learn: When to fine-tune, and what full fine-tuning costs
Catastrophic forgetting and how to limit it
intro.why: Fine-tuning turns a general base model into an assistant or a specialist. Parameter-efficient methods make that affordable on a single GPU and let one base model serve many tasks.

sections.title: Why fine-tune, and full fine-tuning
sections.plain: Further train a pre-trained model on a smaller targeted dataset so it behaves the way you need.
sections.body:
A pre-trained base model predicts plausible continuations; it does not reliably follow instructions or a house style. Fine-tuning continues training on a smaller, curated dataset to specialise behaviour: a format, a task, a domain, a tone, or tool use.

Alternatives first: prompting (M10) costs nothing to try; retrieval (M12) adds fresh facts better than fine-tuning does. Fine-tune when you need consistent behaviour, have many examples, or want a smaller model to match a larger one on one job.

Full fine-tuning updates every parameter. It is the most flexible but inherits the training memory bill (≈16 bytes/param with Adam: 112 GB for 7B before activations), needs one full copy per task, and risks forgetting (below). Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) freezes the base and trains a small number of new parameters.

sections.title: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
sections.plain: Show the model example prompts with ideal answers and train it to produce those answers.
sections.body:
SFT trains on (prompt, response) pairs with the ordinary next-token cross-entropy loss. The prompt tokens are normally masked from the loss, so the model learns to produce responses rather than imitate users.

Worked: "[user] Translate hi to French [assistant] salut [end]". Averaging the loss over all 8 tokens gives 1.250; over the 2 response tokens only, 0.450. Only those two positions produce gradients.

Practical points: quality and diversity beat volume (a few thousand excellent examples can suffice); use the same chat template at training and inference; learning rates are much smaller than in pre-training; train for a few epochs and watch validation loss for overfitting.

sections.title: Instruction fine-tuning
sections.plain: Fine-tune on many different tasks written as instructions, so the model learns to follow instructions in general.
sections.body:
Instruction fine-tuning is SFT on a broad mixture of tasks phrased as natural-language instructions (classify, summarise, translate, extract, reason, code), often with templates like "Instruction / Input / Response" or role-based chat formats.

The key finding: training on many diverse task types lets the model generalise zero-shot to held-out tasks it never saw, because it learns the meta-skill of reading and following instructions. Diversity of instructions and phrasings matters more than many examples of each task; including some step-by-step solutions improves reasoning.

Instruction-tuned models are typically aligned further with human preferences (M9) to become helpful, harmless assistants.

sections.title: Prompt and prefix tuning
sections.plain: Keep the model frozen and learn a few special input vectors that steer it toward the task.
sections.body:
Prompt tuning learns n "virtual token" embeddings prepended to the input (n × d parameters, e.g. 20 × 4096 = 81,920). Prefix tuning learns key and value vectors prepended at every layer (n × L × 2d), giving more control over each layer's attention. P-tuning variants use a small network to generate these vectors.

Benefits: tiny per-task storage, one frozen model serves many tasks, mixed-task batches are easy. Drawbacks: they use up context positions, are sensitive to initialisation and learning rate, and usually trail LoRA on harder tasks, closing the gap mainly on very large models.

sections.title: LoRA
sections.plain: Learn a small low-rank correction to each big weight matrix instead of changing the whole matrix.
sections.body:
Low-Rank Adaptation freezes W and learns an update ΔW = BA with rank r:

$$h = Wx + \frac{\alpha}{r} BAx,\qquad B\in\mathbb R^{d\times r},\ A\in\mathbb R^{r\times k}$$

B starts at zero (so training begins at the base model) and A is random. Trainable parameters: r(d + k).

Worked: r = 8 on a 1000 × 1000 matrix: 8 × 2000 = 16,000 parameters, 1.6% of 1,000,000. A 7B model with r = 16 on the query and value projections of 32 layers trains ≈ 8.4M parameters (0.12%).

Why it works: the weight changes needed for adaptation have low intrinsic rank. After training BA can be added into W, so inference has no extra latency; or many LoRA modules can be kept and swapped per request. Choices: rank (4–64), α, which projections (attention, MLP).

sections.title: QLoRA and adapters
sections.plain: Keep the frozen base in 4-bit to save memory and train LoRA on top; or insert small extra layers called adapters.
sections.body:
QLoRA quantizes the frozen base to 4-bit (NormalFloat4, with double quantization of the scales) and back-propagates through it into 16-bit LoRA matrices; paged optimizer states avoid memory spikes. Memory before activations for 7B: full fine-tuning ≈ 112 GB, LoRA on a 16-bit base ≈ 14 GB, QLoRA ≈ 3.6 GB, enough to fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU with quality close to 16-bit fine-tuning.

Adapters insert small bottleneck modules (down-project → nonlinearity → up-project, with a residual) after attention and/or MLP sub-layers, training about 1–4% of parameters. Unlike merged LoRA, they add a little inference latency because they are extra layers.

sections.title: Model merging and distillation
sections.plain: Combine several fine-tuned models by adding their weight changes, or train a small model to copy a big one.
sections.body:
Model merging combines fine-tuned models sharing a base without more training. A task vector τ = θ_fine-tuned − θ_base; adding several (θ = θ_base + Στᵢ) can combine skills, while simple averaging dilutes them. Interference between task vectors is reduced by trimming small or sign-conflicting changes (TIES, DARE). Toy: base 1, math +0.6, code +0.5 → task-vector merge (1.6, 1.5) vs average (1.3, 1.25).

Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student to match a larger teacher. Soft targets at temperature T reveal the teacher's ranking of wrong answers ("dark knowledge"):

$$\mathcal L = (1-\lambda)\,\text{CE}(y, q) + \lambda\, T^2\, \text{KL}\big(p_T \,\|\, q_T\big)$$

For LLMs, distillation also means generating training data (responses, reasoning traces) with a strong teacher and fine-tuning the student on it.

sections.title: Catastrophic forgetting
sections.plain: Training hard on a new task can wipe out skills the model already had.
sections.body:
Gradient updates for a new task freely overwrite weights that supported old abilities. In code example ex2 a model fitted to task A (error ≈ 0) reaches error 3.37 on A after training on task B. In LLMs, narrow fine-tuning can erode general knowledge, instruction following, other languages or safety behaviour.

Mitigations:

  • Replay / data mixing: include general or earlier-task data (ex2: 20% replay cuts A error to 2.27 in a model too small to fit both).
  • PEFT: LoRA and adapters change far fewer weights, so they forget less (but also learn less).
  • Regularisation toward the original weights (e.g. elastic weight consolidation, KL to the base model).
  • Small learning rates and few epochs; evaluate broadly, not just on the target task.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Fine-tuning is poor at adding facts: models learn new facts slowly and may hallucinate more; retrieval is usually better for knowledge.
  • A little SFT goes a long way: style and format shift with surprisingly few examples.
  • LoRA rank is not quality: higher r doesn't always help; data matters more.
  • Safety can regress after benign fine-tuning; re-run safety evaluations.

code.title: LoRA counts, a learned low-rank update, and QLoRA memory
code.explain: Counts LoRA parameters for r = 4–64 on a 1000 × 1000 matrix (r = 8 → 16,000, 1.6%) and for a 7B model (8.4M, 0.12%), compares memory for full fine-tuning (112 GB), LoRA (14 GB) and QLoRA (3.6 GB), and trains B and A by gradient descent to recover a rank-2 change while W₀ stays frozen.
mistakes: Initialising both B and A randomly (training would not start from the base model).
Forgetting the α/r scaling when merging.
code.code:
"""LoRA parameter counts, a low-rank update learned by gradient descent, and QLoRA memory."""
import numpy as np

d = k = 1000
for r in (4, 8, 16, 64):
    lora = r * (d + k)
    print(f"LoRA r={r:2d} on a {d}x{k} matrix: {lora:,} trainable vs {d*k:,} ({100*lora/(d*k):.1f}%)")

# 7B-style model: LoRA r=16 on query and value projections of 32 layers, width 4096
L, h, r = 32, 4096, 16
lora7 = L * 2 * r * (h + h)
print(f"7B model, LoRA r={r} on Q and V in {L} layers: {lora7/1e6:.1f}M trainable ({100*lora7/7e9:.2f}% of 7B)")

# Memory: full fine-tuning (16 B/param with Adam) vs LoRA (frozen 16-bit base) vs QLoRA (4-bit base)
N = 7e9
full = N * 16
lora_mem = N * 2 + lora7 * 16
qlora = N * 0.5 + lora7 * 16
for name, m in (("full fine-tuning (Adam, fp32 states)", full), ("LoRA, 16-bit frozen base", lora_mem), ("QLoRA, 4-bit frozen base", qlora)):
    print(f"{name:38s}: {m/1e9:6.1f} GB before activations")

# Learn a low-rank update: W_target = W0 + B_true @ A_true (rank 2); fit B @ A with rank 2
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m, rank = 20, 20, 2
W0 = rng.normal(size=(n, m))
dW = rng.normal(size=(n, rank)) @ rng.normal(size=(rank, m)) * 0.3
X = rng.normal(size=(m, 200)); Y = (W0 + dW) @ X
A = rng.normal(size=(rank, m)) * 0.01
B = np.zeros((n, rank))                      # B starts at zero, so training starts from W0 exactly
lr = 0.0004
for step in range(1501):
    E = (W0 + B @ A) @ X - Y
    gW = E @ X.T / X.shape[1]
    gB, gA = gW @ A.T, B.T @ gW
    B -= lr * gB * 50; A -= lr * gA * 50
    if step in (0, 5, 20, 60, 1500):
        print(f"step {step:4d}: loss {np.mean(E**2):.4f}")
print(f"trainable {B.size + A.size} numbers vs {W0.size} in the full matrix; base W0 never changed")

code.title: SFT masking, distillation, merging and forgetting
code.explain: Computes SFT loss over all tokens (1.250) vs response tokens (0.450), distillation KL at T = 1/2/4, task-vector merge vs averaging, and demonstrates catastrophic forgetting (task A error 0 → 3.37) and partial recovery with 20% replay (2.27).
code.code:
"""SFT loss masking, model merging, distillation with temperature, and catastrophic forgetting."""
import numpy as np

# SFT: only response tokens contribute to the loss
tokens = ["[user]", "Translate", "hi", "to", "French", "[assistant]", "salut", "[end]"]
mask = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1]
nll = [2.1, 3.0, 1.2, 0.8, 1.9, 0.1, 0.7, 0.2]
full = np.mean(nll)
masked = sum(n for n, m in zip(nll, mask) if m) / sum(mask)
print("SFT example:", " ".join(f"{t}{'*' if m else ''}" for t, m in zip(tokens, mask)), "(* = trained)")
print(f"loss over all tokens {full:.3f}; loss over response tokens only {masked:.3f}")

# Distillation: soften teacher logits with temperature, match with KL
def softmax(z, T=1): z = np.asarray(z) / T; e = np.exp(z - z.max()); return e / e.sum()
teacher = [4.0, 2.0, 1.0, -1.0]
student = [3.0, 2.5, 0.0, 0.0]
for T in (1, 2, 4):
    p, q = softmax(teacher, T), softmax(student, T)
    kl = np.sum(p * np.log(p / q))
    print(f"T={T}: teacher {np.round(p, 3)}  KL(teacher||student) = {kl:.4f}")
print("higher T exposes the teacher's ranking of wrong answers (dark knowledge)")

# Model merging: task arithmetic on toy weight vectors
base = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
task_math = base + np.array([0.6, 0.0, 0.0, 0.1])
task_code = base + np.array([0.0, 0.5, 0.0, -0.1])
merged = base + (task_math - base) + (task_code - base)
avg = (task_math + task_code) / 2
print("task-vector merge:", merged, " simple average:", avg)

# Catastrophic forgetting: fit task A, then task B; measure error on A; then with 20% replay
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def data(w, n=200): X = rng.normal(size=(n, 5)); return X, X @ w
wA, wB = rng.normal(size=5), rng.normal(size=5)
XA, yA = data(wA); XB, yB = data(wB)
def train(w, X, y, steps=300, lr=0.05):
    for _ in range(steps): w = w - lr * X.T @ (X @ w - y) / len(y)
    return w
mse = lambda w, X, y: float(np.mean((X @ w - y) ** 2))
w = train(np.zeros(5), XA, yA)
print(f"after task A: error on A {mse(w, XA, yA):.3f}")
w1 = train(w, XB, yB)
print(f"after task B only: error on A {mse(w1, XA, yA):.3f}, on B {mse(w1, XB, yB):.3f}  <- forgetting")
Xm = np.vstack([XB, XA[:50]]); ym = np.concatenate([yB, yA[:50]])
w2 = train(w, Xm, ym)
print(f"task B with 20% replay of A: error on A {mse(w2, XA, yA):.3f}, on B {mse(w2, XB, yB):.3f}")
print("(one small linear model cannot fit two conflicting tasks perfectly; replay trades a little B accuracy for much less forgetting of A)")
